{{short description|American mathematician}}
'''Arthur Sard''' (28 July 1909, [[New York City]] &ndash; 31 August 1980, [[Basel]]) was an American mathematician, famous for his work in [[differential topology]] and in [[spline interpolation]]. His fame stems primarily from [[Sard's theorem]], which says that the set of [[Critical point (mathematics)|critical value]]s of a differential function which has sufficiently many derivatives has measure zero.<ref name="in memoriam" />

== Life and career ==
Arthur Sard was born and grew up in New York City and spent most of his adult life there. He attended the [[Friends Seminary]], a private school in [[Manhattan]], and went to college at [[Harvard University]], where he received in 1931 his bachelor's degree, in 1932 his master's degree, and in 1936 his PhD under the direction of [[Marston Morse]].<ref name="in memoriam" /> Sard's PhD thesis has the title ''The measure of the critical values of functions''.<ref>''Notes.'' In: ''Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society.'' Vol. 43, No. 5, 1937, {{ISSN|1088-9485}}, ([https://www.ams.org/journals/bull/1937-43-05/S0002-9904-1937-06523-2/S0002-9904-1937-06523-2.pdf PDF])</ref> He was a member of the first faculty members at the then newly founded [[Queens College, City University of New York|Queens College]], where he worked from 1937 to 1970.<ref name="in memoriam" />

During WWII Sard worked as a member, under the auspices of the [[Applied Mathematics Panel]], of the ''Applied Mathematics Group'' of [[Columbia University]] (AMG-C), especially in support of [[Fire-control system|fire control]] for machine guns mounted on [[bomber]]s. [[Saunders Mac Lane]] wrote concerning Sard: “His judicious judgments kept AMG-C on a straight course, […]”.<ref>Saunders Mac Lane: ''Requiem for the Skillful.'' In: ''Notices of the American Mathematical Society.'' Vol. 44, No. 2, 1997, {{ISSN|0002-9920}}, pp. 207–208 ([https://www.ams.org/notices/199702/comm-maclane.pdf PDF; 43 kB]).</ref>

Sard retired as professor emeritus in 1970 at Queens College and then worked at [[La Jolla]], where he spent five years as a research associate in the mathematics department of the [[University of California, San Diego]]. In 1975 he went to [[Binningen, Switzerland|Binningen]] near [[Basel]] and taught at various European universities and research institutes. In 1978 he accepted an invitation from the Soviet Academy of Sciences to be a guest lecturer.  In 1978 and 1979 he was a guest professor at the [[University of Siegen]]. Arthur Sard died on 31 August 1980 in Basel.<ref name="in memoriam" />

From 1938 until his death Sard published almost forty research articles in [[Academic journal|refereed mathematical journal]]s.<ref name="amm" /> Also he wrote two [[monograph]]s: in 1963 the book ''Linear Approximation'' and in 1971, in collaboration with Sol Weintraub, ''A Book of Splines''.<ref name="amm" /> According to the book review from the [[Deutsche Mathematiker-Vereinigung]] the content-rich („inhaltsreiche“) ''Linear Approximation'' is an important contribution to the theory of approximation of integrals, derivatives, function values, and sums („ein wesentlicher Beitrag zur Theorie der Approximation von Integralen, Ableitungen, Funktionswerten und Summen“).<ref>Manfred v. Golitschek, Paul Otto Runck: ''A. Sard, Linear Approximation.'' In: ''Jahresbericht der Deutschen Mathematiker-Vereinigung'', Nr. 73, B. G. Teubner Verlag, Stuttgart 1971/72, {{ISSN|0012-0456}}, S. 31–33 ([http://www.digizeitschriften.de/main/dms/img/?PPN=PPN37721857X_0073 online] from [[:de:DigiZeitschriften|DigiZeitschriften]] in German)</ref>

== Works ==
Sard published thirty-eight research articles and the two following monographs:
* Arthur Sard: ''Linear approximation.'' 2nd edn. [[American Mathematical Society]], Providence, Rhode Island 1963, {{ISBN|0-8218-1509-1}} (''Mathematical Surveys and Monographs.'' Vol. 9).
* Arthur Sard, Sol Weintraub: ''A Book of Splines.'' [[John Wiley & Sons|John Wiley & Sons Inc]], New York 1971, {{ISBN|0-471-75415-3}}
